review:
Ghostwire Tokyo is a perfectly average game, never really excelling at any of its elements but being just enjoyable enough to see through to the end. 

The game is set in a deserted Tokyo that has been consumed by supernatural forces. We play as Akito, a teenager who survives the event due to being inhabited by a spirit named KK. Akito gains mystical abilities and sets out to unravel the mystery behind the city's mass disappearance. 

I was incredibly excited to play this game set in a location I love and influenced by folklore and urban legends I am most interested in. Unfortunately, it barely scratches the surface with this aspect, which I found to be odd considering what the game is about. 

I felt this sentiment pretty much across the board with my playthrough. It's like the bones are there, but there's just no real meat to it. Everything seems to be put together in a very basic way, without trying to delve deeper and develop these aspects past surface level. That doesn't mean to say that the game is bad, not at all. It just doesn't feel like it really nails anything. 

The story is pretty short, and the map is absolutely littered with all sorts of collectibles, side quests, special items, fast travel points, and whatever else they could cram. I don't usually have an issue with collectibles but when the story only takes about 12 hours there is an expectation on the player to keep pouring hours in to mindless running around collecting without any real payoff. 

I wish Steam had a neutral review option as I don't feel particularly strongly about my experience being positive or negative, just fine. 

5/10

Ghostwire Tokyo is an open world first person action game. Tokyo has been covered in a strange fog that caused all the citizens to disappear, and supernatural creatures are wandering the streets.

The only person still alive is player character Akito, who gained magical powers when his body was taken over by a mysterious spirit called KK, and now they must work together to figure out how to save the city.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

•	Combat is like a first person shooter but instead of guns you can use three magic attacks (wind, water, fire), a bow, and you can sneak up behind most enemies to perform a melee takedown. Wind is like a basic pistol, it has good range but does low damage so you need to hit enemies several times to kill them. Water is a wave attack that functions a bit like a shotgun, but the range is so short that its only really worth using indoors. Fire can be charged up into an AoE fireball attack that can kill multiple enemies in the blast radius, so this is the most enjoyable ability to use, but it also has the lowest spirit energy (ammo) capacity.

•	Enemies have a unique visual design, and include faceless businessmen holding umbrellas, headless schoolgirls, women with long hair wielding giant scissors, floating ghosts, and more.

•	Open world is similar to Ubisoft’s design style of covering the map with dozens of icons for the player to clear. Most side quests only take a few minutes to complete and contain a minimal amount of story.

•	The city is covered by a fog that drains your health. You can cleanse Torii gates to clear fog from the surrounding area, allowing you to access those parts of the map.

•	Throughout the city you’ll find civilian souls floating in the air. You can use paper dolls to absorb them and then upload to safety through public phone booths (this game is quite strange). There are 240,000 souls and each group you save contains roughly 100-200, so you can imagine how many there are scattered all over the map like a typical open world collectable item.

•	Some Torii gates and souls are located on rooftops, which will please fans of Ubisoft tower climbing. You can use a grapple on some flying creatures to gain height and you can do a Batman style glide for a few seconds to jump between buildings. Sometimes there isn’t an obvious way up so getting to the roof is more like a puzzle.

•	While there doesn’t seem to be any Humans alive in the city, there are lots of dogs. You can use KK’s power to telepathically read the dogs’ thoughts and then give them food. To thank you they’ll dig up some coins or help you find shrines which increase your spirit energy limits. Coins can be used to buy consumable items at shops run by spirit cats. (Did I mention that this game is really strange?)

[h1]Story[/h1]

•	Main story has an interesting premise but is let down by a weak villain whose plan makes less sense the more you learn about it. Side quests mostly involve helping spirits deal with problems caused by supernatural creatures so they can move on to the afterlife.

[h1]Technical[/h1]

•	I had some framerate issues until I switched textures from cinematic to automatic. Not sure exactly what that does, I couldn’t see a quality difference, but it did stabilise framerate.

•	I didn’t encounter any bugs or crashes.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work well with mouse and keyboard.

•	Took me 16 hours to complete the main story and most side quests. I think I collected around 100,000 souls.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

After my 7 hours of playtime, I decided to update my review by rewriting most of it.

[i]TL; DR at the bottom.[/i]

First of all, I picked up this game because it is not horror. If you are expecting the game to be creepy and give off a horror vibe, then this game is not for you. Judging from watching the trailer, which is pretty much clear. I have always been wanting to try a game that involves ghosts or supernatural beings, but most of them ended up being a horror, which I hate mainly because of jump scares.

About the story, I believe I have not yet advanced that far in the story so I would rather not judge much about this. All I could say was the story starts off quickly, with neither good nor bad meaning. The cinematic looks good though.

Next, the combat mechanics resembles a first-person shooter-style with special skills and gears, skills upgrading mechanic included. The overall combat mechanics are fresh and new to me. The combat may seem not complex, but from my playing experience, good timing and shots accuracy are what you need in this game, which is what made this game somewhat more challenging.

The graphics are pretty much detailed. Walking around the city looking at things is quite a good experience for me. You can even read texts on almost every billboard. With Ray Tracing on, reflections on water puddles and wet floors look surprisingly stunning. Only graphics drawbacks are a-bit-ugly raindrops, blurry mirror reflection, and no self-reflection.

The performance is kind of good. With medium Ray Tracing and balanced DLSS settings, the game is able is perform at around 90-130 FPS with my RTX 3070 Ti on a 2k monitor.

One of the downsides of the game I have experienced is the lack of soundtracks. Most of the time, there is just no BGM. Everything is quiet during exploration. BGM only plays during combat as far as I remember, they are not my type, but they really fit the game. Another downside is that I feel minor dizziness when I do at 30-minute of playtime. This is rare for me, but I would like to note this in my review just in case.

Lastly, you can pet and feed dogs in the game. It seems like you can also pet cats in the game, I have tried it, but the actions do not really look like petting. My only complaints are that the dog model quality is not as high as I expected and I wish for more dog breeds other than different colors of Shiba.

[i]TL; DR: I like it because the game is not horror and contains no jump scares. FPS-style combat with special skills. Detailed graphics, just a few flaws. Good performance. Lacks BGM. May experience minor dizziness. Can pet dogs.[/i]

Climb the towers... sorry, cleanse the Torii gates to reveal the map. Sure is impressive that Mr Badguy hid these gates in plot-convenient groupings!

The plot is very... Japanese. Lots of cutscenes of standing there alternately striking a dynamic pose whilst yelling for someone to explain themselves then acting like they don't understand and would like clarification. Nani? Time to charge headfirst towards the enemy with an attack pose and BAM oh no you got flown backwards! And Mr Badguy has very tenuous motivations for doing what he's doing,

I guess ultimately it has some pretty basic ideas that don't *quite* gel together into something that could have been incredible, even though the potential was there. As above, worth checking out if you think it might appeal to you, but this is very much a tempered recommendation.

[h1]A Good Game, But It Hard To Tell What It Wants To Be.[/h1]

The first time I saw Ghostwire: Tokyo I really thought this game was the survival horror Tango Gameworks were well-known for, but set in Japan. When I finally get my hands on it, well, let`s just say the experience is quite different than my initial thoughts. It is not a bad game. In fact, Ghostwire: Tokyo has, in my opinion, best open world design after Elden Ring and Witcher 3. The animation is smooth and satisfying to watch. And the core gameplay has that vibe of classic survival horror Shinji Mikami made in the past. Yet, lacking a defining theme and being too conservative are the two reason that put the game in an awkward situation. It is hard to say the game is bad, and it is also hard to say it is a must-play either.

[h1]Things I Like About Ghostwire: Tokyo:[/h1]

[b]1. Open World[/b]
I am still amazed at the game's open world design. The level of detail is insane, an almost one to one rendition of Shibuya according to my sisiter. Simply taking a stoll down the street constantly fills me with wonder. No scenes has been copy-pasted blatantly. Every part of this city has its own special sense of style, which make exploration really great in Ghostwire: Tokyo. The experience only elevates with the ability Spectral Vision, a radar-like skill which highlights items and enemies around you. Pick a direction, drop the Spectral Vision, and go forth at your leisure. You would be surprised how much secrets you can uncover from  doing this. It also serves as a great reminder if the density of the city may be too overwhelming.

[b]2. Yokai, Obessesion, And Urban Legneds[/b]
Ghostwire: Tokyo does a great job at portraying the spiritual belief of east-asia, in the form of side quests. Classic yokai like Zashiki-warashi, Nekomata, and more make their appearances in game. Several side quests paint a clear vision of how obessesion can cause serious trouble to one`s mental and physical health state. And my favorite parts: the game`s rendition of urban legends. Two of them stand out the most. Kuchisake and Kisaragi Station are the highlight of my playthrough. Not only the atmosphere is horrifyingly superb, but also their presentation leave quite a impact, really making me wish this game is a full on horror.

[b]3. Other Compliments[/b]
→Sound cue is really distinguished and well-done. 
→Hand gesture animation is smooth and satisfying to watch.
→Using cats' thought as hint is a interesting idea.

[h1]Things I Dislike About Ghostwire: Tokyo:[/h1]

[b]1. Upgrade System Is Conservative[/b]
I always view upgrade system as evolution for the core gamplay, branching paths for players to customize their playstyle. So I am really disappointed to find out the upgrade system is rather conservative. It never goes beyond offering you minor convenience like faster casting, crouch-walking speed increase, etc. The spell upgrades just make you fire faster, wider, and bigger. It`s a shame because there are so many potentials the dev can put in, ideas like implementing elemental damage instead of just visual indicators, fusing two of the three spells to create either unique attacks, buffs or debuffs, or even something for Wired-in that can create a doppelganger mirroring the protagonist.

[b]2. Survival? Horror?[/b]
Another main problem of Ghostwire: Tokyo is that it`s hard to pinpoint what the game is trying to be. My first impression of the game is "Evil Within-like sets in modern Japan", so I am really fixated on regarding this game as survival horror. Unfortunately, Ghostwire: Tokyo fails to meet both. Survival is never a problem considering the abundant resource scattering around the city. In fact it`s pretty hard to run out of resource in this game. The horror part, on the other hand, comes really close to great, if they can stretch it to the full game. Like I said before, the side quests involving urban legends have some of the best setup for horror. Horrifying atmosphere, terrifying yet mesmerizing visuals and a suitable difficulty. It pains me to see that the dev doesn`t bring that level of horror buildup to the whole game.

[b]3. Other Complaints[/b]
→The later parts of the story feel rushed.
→Boss fights are disappointingly easy despite their striking visuals.
→Wish there are more yokai introduced.

At it's core, it's a beautiful and well polished game, with enjoyable combat, an amazing atmosphere, and a lot of unique ideas.  It focuses around Japanese folklore, which normally I don't care about, but it makes each new discovery interesting.  

It then adds on a huge amount of collectibles of various types, randomly hidden all throughout the city, which improve your character in some way - which can be discouraging for some, but I found it engaging



Unfortunately, that's part of the problem; I did a lot of the sidequests, and collected a lot of things.  I'm now 8 hours in and have fully upgraded all my combat abilities, and I don't think there's really anywhere left to go.  This is what combat is going to be like for the next 30 hours or so.  
Which is sorta fine, because it's still enjoyable, but I'm not sure it will be enjoyable 30 hours later.  


Otherwise, many of the quests are also very hollow; they exist only to show you some creature from folklore, and then you hold down the 'absorb power' button and it dies and you get a reward.

The rewards also stop feeling rewarding when you see that after 8 hours of meticulously grabbing every one you find, you're at 20,000/250,000

This makes the collectible business trivial and tedious; every few steps you stop, press the hotkey, look around/up/down/everywhere, try to figure out if any of the dozen outlines currently being shown are anything useful, move forward a few more steps, repeat



So, it's a maybe for me.  I still plan to keep going with it, and just avoid/ignore the collectibles, and see how it all plays out.  And on its surface, it really does look and feel great.  I just have suspicions that it can't keep up the pace for another 30 hours, especially now that my tech tree is already basically full

In this game, you pet cats, then you buy dog food from other cats (sadly un-pettable) to give to dogs, which you also pet. You can pet every dog and cat as many times as you want, and you can also listen to what they're thinking. 

To buy the dog food, you need money, which you can often find in the trash. Tokyo is a very clean city where trash is deposited in appropriate receptacles, so it's very easy to find it. You can also get money by destroying ghostly money jars and ghostly lucky cat statues, which are everywhere. Another way to get money is absorbing spirits into little paper dolls (available from cursed shrines that you purify) and then uploading them to the internet from a payphone. 

Sometimes really angry spirits try to stop your quest for dog food money, and then you have to fight them, but it's worth it.

In short Ghostwire Tokyo a good game: definitely overhyped and not as good as it was built up, but neither is it horrible or lacking any depth.  Its a difficult game to recommend as it is so polarizing, all in I'd say its a good "wait for a sale" kinda game; throw it on the wishlist and forget about it till you get the email.

It's real issue is that each of its good elements is offset by some flaw:
The wonderful spooky atmosphere is countered by the open world, letting you just escape to the roofs and avoid the oppressive environment
The creative element of the combat (element weaving) is let down by the lack of variety or real progression
The interesting world building is deflated by the lackluster story/characters

Its a passion project, clearly made with love with GORGEOUS visuals, that ran out of something (likely time and money) and ended up having content cut and the story rushed.

Ghostwire was semi-panned at release for its repetitive structure, shallow combat, and dull writing — absolutely fair criticisms. What elevates the game beyond other open-world fare is its lucid-dreamlike quality and japanophile value.

First, the downsides: Almost all of Ghostwire's interactions boil down to reaching a location to collect something, or initiating a combat encounter to then collect something afterward. Any single event you encounter in the game will be copy-pasted across its urban world a dozen times or more.  The writing is mind-numbing boilerplate; the generic protagonist needs to save his underwritten damsel in distress from a nihilistic badguy who wields occult powers that plunge the world into darkness. The sidequests as well are similarly bland, though there are a few visually imaginative highlights. The combat has a certain workflow that, once you learn it, never changes. I've played blockbuster open world games that have offered more depth, complexity, interest and serendipity like Watch Dogs 2 and Red Dead Redemption 2; on those "objective" measures, Ghostwire doesn't hold a candle.

What makes Ghostwire intoxicating is its dreamlike quality: wandering the abandoned, rain-soaked back-alleys of Japan; gliding from rooftop to rooftop in search of the city's lost spirits; I often have dreams like this. The game takes place in an apocalyptic Shibuya where its denizens have been spirited away, while the creatures of Japanese mythology haunt the city. Its many collect-a-thon mechanics lead you on a tour of its virtual Japan. Sidequests have you investigate hauntings of residences, shrines, offices, graveyards, bathhouses, and so on. The game begins in obligatory locations like the Shibuya Scramble, but eventually fans out into highways, rivers, public apartment blocks, sleepy suburbs, shopping arcades, and even a rendition of Yanaka Ginza. (It's adherence to real-life Shibuya is pretty loose — its world is more of a greatest-hits of broader Tokyo, and one setpiece I suspect is pulled from a certain shrine in Kyoto.)

If you have a Japanophile button in you, expect Ghostwire to mash it vigorously. That may be a requirement to enjoying the game, even moreso than the Yakuza / Like a Dragon series. If you're burned out on those, but need something to scratch that same itch, Ghostwire could fit the bill.

Being honest, Ghostwire is not an amazing game, yet it's densely realized world and exploration focus scratches a similar 'virtual tourism' itch that games like Yakuza and Persona do. It's a deep dive into japanese culture while also being a fantasy of exploring an empty Shibuya scramble, which would normally be swarming with people.

The combat is ok and the collectaton nature is kinda generic, but goddamn this is an beatiful, detailed world that is very fun to explore.

[i]Ghostwire: Tokyo[/i] is a supernatural open-world exploration / action game that takes place in a fictional Shibuya (a municipality of Tokyo) whose inhabitants have all mysteriously vanished after the city has been overtaken by malevolent ghostly entities.

You play as Akito, a young man who wakes up in the middle of the iconic Shibuya crossing in the aftermath of a major car crash. With Akito being at the edge between life and death, an unfamiliar spirit suddenly enters his body, preventing him from passing away, thus allowing him to remain connected to this world and to witness for the first time the parade of “Visitors” unleashing a catastrophic fog that wipes out most of Tokyo’s population. The Visitors are an army of ghastly beings that came to invade the city with the goal of separating people’s spirits from their own bodies and collecting them for nefarious purposes that are revealed a bit later in the game. Somehow Akito manages to outlive this event by staying hidden from their sight, thus becoming the sole survivor of this cataclysm.

While reluctant at first about teaming up, Akito and the entity that inhabits him (called “KK”) soon discover that they both seek revenge on a common enemy and that they ultimately pursue the same goal: stopping the enemy attack on Tokyo. The actual orchestrator of the invasion and thus the main antagonist of the game, Hannya, is the target that KK and his team used to pursue in his former life as a cop, but also the one who kidnapped Akito’s hospitalized sister to use her as a catalyst in an occult ritual. KK needs a body in order to achieve his purpose of stopping Hannya, while Akito needs to stay alive long enough to save his sister from Hannya’s hands. As the game progresses, the duo starts warming up to each other and eventually end up developing a strong bond based on mutual trust.

By accepting KK as his inhabitant, Akito can use KK’s supernatural powers to fight off evil. These are ethereal spells based on the wind / fire / water elements, used as basic attacks, but they can also be charged up for increased damage or range. Apart from these 3 main spells, there’s not much else to employ during a fight. Akito can also use a bow (with a very limited amount of arrows), but it also requires to be charged up first before releasing the shot. There are a few talisman types - one-time consumables that act as location-targeted spells (for example, a mass stun, or something that produces a bush you can hide into). The talismans as well as the arrows can’t be picked up from the environment (with very rare exceptions for arrows), therefore they have to constantly be replenished by buying them from one of the many shops. The three main spells have an ammunition system, and you replenish their charges by destroying glitchy objects in the game world.

While other reviews complain that the fighting system is rather minimalistic, this was one of my motivations for picking up the game. I wanted to play something with rather uncomplicated fighting mechanics, so I can enjoy it without the stress of mashing several buttons in a row, trying to get those combos up and running. And [i]Ghostwire: Tokyo[/i] provided that relaxing experience I was expecting, although I have to admit that in some areas things got a bit tougher when a bunch of piled up enemies kept stunning and interrupting Akito’s spell casting. Overall the fighting aspect of the game felt fairly easy, without being completely unchallenging.

[i]Ghostwire: Tokyo[/i] is more of a collectathon rather than anything else. I’ve never seen more collectibles in a game than here. Not only that there are several kinds of them (with a few dozen items in each category), but take for example the requirement to gather 240.300 spirits in order to save them from being collected by Hannya. Apart from side missions or some other events that award you 500 - 1000 spirits, most of these are gathered in batches of 100. I’ll let you do the math, which will probably lead you to the same conclusion that I reached after 50 hours of running around for all these: that the game is more or less a completionism hell. Although designed in a way that allows you to pursue solely the main story (which by the way, takes around 6-10h in its bare form - as my rough estimate) and perhaps engaging yourself in minimal gathering actions, I found it pretty important to do the latter more extensively because a lot of these items will increase your spell charge capacity or allow you to unlock new skills. On the other hand, the enemies seemed to somewhat scale with my character, so in hindsight I would say that while the game lets you decide whether to first go for unlocks and upgrades to increase your damage output, it only confers a moderate advantage.

Having tons of collectibles in a game can seem frustrating for some. Especially if one wants to gather them all, it takes a lot of patience and repetitive actions. However, I didn’t mind it too much. What I did mind though was how hard the collectibles were to spot without a guide (and I am in awe of those who spent hours creating them). There's a hotkey to highlight the silhouettes of the most important objects in a 50m area for a few seconds, so you will be pressing this very often to highlight your enemies or other beings from the shadowy world. Most of the highlighted items are the ones you can destroy for recharging your spells, and the collectibles you seek are typically very tiny, so even after hours of gameplay and learning by heart the possible shapes of the objects to charge your spells, I still found it completely useless for spotting collectibles, except at very close range.

The map is gigantic, leaving a lot of space for exploration. The amount of detail is astonishing, and the reconstruction of the city is absolutely remarkable. The streets are empty, devoid of people, which creates an eerie atmosphere, especially because the worn clothes left behind make it look like the bodies have all been swept away in an instant. Completely opposite of this stillness there’s the aliveness of the colorful lit-up billboards hanging on the buildings of a convoluted shopping plaza or on very tall office towers / apartment blocks, reminiscent of a once very active and crowded city. The atmosphere and the design of the world is in my opinion the strongest aspect of [i]Ghostwire: Tokyo[/i].

The game is considered to belong to the horror genre. As a person who is especially sensitive to anything that is scary or gives an uneasy feeling, I can assure you that it’s tremendously mild on that scale, even close to 0. Since the enemies explode into crystals when they are killed, there is no gore in the game. There are no jump scares and the enemy design is not frightening - Akito will mostly fight slenderman-like creatures, headless but cheerful schoolgirls or office clerks - nothing that can really give you nightmares. Some side missions will have you explore a haunted house, and unforeseen occult things happening there or the unexpected way the level shifts into something else can somewhat give you chills on the spine, but none of this is deeply daunting.

Both the enemies and the collectibles showcase Japanese folklore, however the story felt overall very predictable and generic, in a way that it didn't seem to employ the Asian techniques of storytelling; not only that it has a lot of plot holes and inconsistencies, but overall it seemed to lack that indistinguishable Asian touch, even though it was developed by a Japanese studio.

With its exquisite visuals and detail-rich world, supernatural theme, and fairly relaxed combat, [i]Ghostwire: Tokyo[/i] was all-in-all a great buy for me. I did expect more depth and cohesiveness from the story and would have liked a built-in collectible tracking system, but none of these things hindered my enjoyment too much. Overall, I loved the game as a whole.

As an action-adventure game built around Japanese folklore and urban legends, Ghostwire: Tokyo actually has a pretty interesting premise. Replacing traditional firearms with gesture-based elemental attacks, while mixing in spirits, talismans, bows, and other mechanics, gives the game a combat system that is instantly recognizable and distinct. Unfortunately, the game once again falls into the same open-world formulaic trap that plagued The Evil Within 2.

The combat system looks fairly diverse, with plenty of weapons and tools to choose from. The problem is that it never develops the kind of meaningful tactical decision-making found in games like Resident Evil or The Evil Within. As the protagonist levels up, their abilities quickly become overpowered, turning the enemies from potentially threatening opponents into little more than punching bags. Naturally, combat only gets more repetitive and tedious as the game goes on.

The early game puts a lot of effort into showing off deserted streets, bizarre weather, supernatural encounters, and a huge amount of visual material drawn from Japanese folklore. And honestly, it works pretty well. The atmosphere is one of the strongest parts of the game—at least at first. Unfortunately, as the campaign progresses, increasingly frequent combat encounters slowly drain that atmosphere away. By the end, Ghostwire: Tokyo becomes something of a hollow open-world package that is neither particularly scary nor especially atmospheric.

And speaking of open-world bloat, the open-world structure only makes the game's problems more obvious. Tokyo often feels like a city that is designed to look rich rather than actually offer meaningful variety. The map is packed with repetitive collectibles, purification activities, and combat encounters, while genuinely unique experiences that can meaningfully change how you play are few and far between.

If Tango had taken the time to refine the core gameplay and cut the experience down to a carefully curated linear adventure, Ghostwire: Tokyo could have been one of the standout games in the Japanese urban-horror genre. But once again, Tango took an absolutely fantastic premise and turned it into a boring open-world checklist.

[h1][i]Ghostwire: Tokyo – Beautiful, Boring, and Full of Spirits [/i][/h1]

Ghostwire: Tokyo is a cool looking game, and while I [i]want[/i] to recommend it, I personally didn’t vibe with it. As much as I hate leaving a negative review, I went ahead and did everything the game had to offer even got 100% achievements.

The world itself is a densely packed version of Tokyo, and it’s clear a lot of effort went into making it visually striking. But because of the narrative choice to have no living NPCs, the world often feels empty. At no point did I feel any real sense of awe or a strong desire to explore and immerse myself in the world. 

[h3][b]Story[/b][/h3]
I really enjoyed the side quests, some were exceptionally fun, like the haunted school mission. But the main story was just [b]okay[/b]. Not bad, not great, and ultimately not very memorable. If you’re into Japanese occult themes, this game might be right up your alley.

On paper, Ghostwire’s narrative has some cool ingredients a mysterious fog wipes out Tokyo’s population, leaving only spirits behind. A masked villain is performing strange rituals, and your character, Akito, ends up sharing a body with a grumpy ghost detective named KK. You team up to rescue your sister and stop the masked villain.

That sounds great, right? But the execution is... meh. It quickly turns into a pretty standard "stop the villain who keeps getting stronger while you run errands around town" storyline. There's little emotional payoff, and the pacing is uneven, spending hours cleansing shrines or chasing tanukis really kills the tension. 

[h3][b]Gameplay[/b][/h3]
This is where the game lost me. [b]I just didn’t enjoy it.[/b] The loop is repetitive, and while some might vibe with it, I found it to be a [b]chore[/b], and even though you unlock cool looking powers, they don’t evolve enough to keep things interesting. Even pushing for 100% completion felt genuinely unfun, I had to force myself to finish, hoping it would eventually click. It didn’t.

The [b]combat[/b] also didn’t click with me. There’s not much depth, and it just doesn’t feel good to fight. Enemies are basic and repetitive, making the whole experience feel lackluster. I constantly found myself just wanting to end fights quickly rather than actually enjoying them.  

[h3][b]Spider’s Thread DLC[/b][/h3]
This free DLC introduces a roguelike mode, but I didn’t find it engaging. You’re forced to regrind the same abilities from the main game, and the final boss is just a rehash of the original. It honestly felt like a rushed, low-effort Roblox mod (which, honestly, might be more fun). The only standout was a few new beads that offered buffs but that wasn’t enough to carry it.

[h2][b]❌Technical Issues[/b][/h2]

🔻[b]Stuttering[/b] 
- The game is mostly optimized, but I experienced stutters every few minutes, with FPS randomly dropping by 40-50% for a few seconds, restarting the game usually fixes it. It's not loading assets either, it just randomly drops even if you are doing nothing.

🔻[b]Blurry Graphics (Chromatic Aberration Issue)[/b]
- Even if you turn off Chromatic Aberration in the settings, the game still looks blurry. The only way to fix this is by changing DPI settings manually.  

How to Fix the Blurry Graphics (DPI Scaling Fix):  
1. Find the game’s .exe → C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Ghostwire Tokyo  
2. Right-click → Properties  
3. Go to Compatibility → Click "Change high DPI settings" 
4. Check "Override high DPI scaling behavior", then set it to Application  
5. Click OK and apply changes.  

[h2][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/h2]    
Ghostwire: Tokyo is one of those games that looks amazing in trailers and screenshots, but once you actually play it, the magic fades it lacks the fun factor. For some people, especially fans of Japanese folklore or slower-paced supernatural games, this might still be enjoyable.
If you can grab it at a deep discount, maybe give it a shot. But I picked it up at 50% off, and honestly I still feel like I overpaid.

MY THOUGHTS: I'm not going to lie, the intro scene of this game actually hooked me right off the bat- and that hook stayed with me to the very end of the game. So many times throughout my gameplay I thought "what is going on?!" So they hit the nail on the head with that. It's a very beautiful and artistic game, I love the funky art and designs. The monsters are actually kind of scary. However, there aren't really any jump scares (even though I spent the first hour or so waiting for one- Ya can't help it with how creepy and liminal the buildings feel while inside). It amazes me that this game is 4 years old and the graphics are still very beautiful. The game overall drenched me in curiosity, and I actually learned a little bit about Japanese folklore along the way which was super cool. If you do not know, this is basically a "ghost hunting" game. Instead of weapons, you have ethereal powers + a bow and arrows. 

ABOUT THE GAMEPLAY: This game is STORY HEAVY, and is downright beautiful. The game DOES offer difficulty modes- you can set the game to easy if you are more of a story person, but you can also set it on one of the harder difficulties if you love combat. Regardless, you will still experience a fair amount of combat. The game has 6 chapters, and if you aim for the main storyline alone, you can complete it in about 12-15 hours. (I read online that full completion to 100% can take anywhere between 30-40 hours.) However, there are PLENTY of side missions and quests from lost spirits that will hike your gameplay hours up way further if you like the exploring. There are also hidden items and things to find scattered all around town, "collections to complete" I should say... and even toy capsule machines. Completing certain collections unlocks different camera filters, emojis and more. If you take your time, you will spend a lot of your time exploring both the streets AND the rooftops of "abandoned" Tokyo. cleansing souls and capturing them in an effort to escort them to safety via a telephone booth (Ghostwire... You're literally wiring souls.) You will unlock more locations in the map as you cleanse the Torii gates and "remove" the mysterious fog surrounding you. The side quests are typically simple and some are actually pretty funny. They are worth playing in my opinion, in order to get the full experience. Throughout the game, you will slowly figure out what's going on and begin to understand the story more and more as you progress just like a lot of game, but for me personally? I still questioned the entirety of what was going on for the majority of the game. This really is a "WTF is happening" game... and a "WTF IS THAT!!!!" game. Oh, and you can talk to animals/read their thoughts too... That's pretttttyyyyy dope. (So remember to feed the doggies then follow them to get a little reward!) Overall, I'd rate this game about a 6 or 7 out of 10. It's not the absolute BEST, but it's worth playing- ESPECIALLY if you get it on sale. I bought the game on discount at 90% off, and I am shocked at the quality + amount of gameplay I received for that price. 

***Let it be noted that at some point in chapter 4, you will reach a point of no return until you finish the game which means you will not be able to complete any side quests or anything until you finish the main storyline. So take as much or as little time as you want depending on your level of enjoyment and MAKE SURE YOU VISIT THE CAT VENDORS TO STAY STOCKED UP ON ARROWS (for non-ethereal damage) & SNACKS (for hp).*** Yes, I said cat vendors.

Well... I liked most of the game. But, as many other reviewers who are trying to be somewhat on point, I need to start with the major turn-offs.

First, the game is based on Japanese culture. You may not be a fan, but at least it should not put you off by default. Because some players can't stand games with too much J-stuff.

Second, the game consists majorly of clearing off the map by travelling and searching for collectibles, and constant random fights with respawning enemies, and both of these can be frustrating, not because of their difficulty, but primarily due to the drawn-out and repetitive nature of the process. You can skip some of it, if you're not hunting the complete badge, but it can still wear you out somewhere between story chapters.

Speaking of the story, well... It has its moments, but surely it does not go deep enough, especially if you're skipping the secondary objectives and stuff. 

Finally, if you're aiming for achievements, there's some additional content, called Spider's Thread, and it's a bunch of levels not connected with the main story and organized by random rogue-like principle. That's where the game is really magnifying its weakest sides: zero point one percent story and motivation, 99 point 9 percent repetitive combat and grind. While there were some peculiar levels with changed perspective (the main game has only one or two such sequences, but it is a really cool experience), most of grind time in Spider's Thread is totally fruitless and disengaging.

Now, I think I said enough to provide the base for the point why Ghostwire: Tokyo met with a rather cool reception, both from pro critics and common players, upon release.

However... If you'll skip it, you lose a totally unique experience of a modern ninja-ghosthunter, with bizarre magic shooting fighting system, and full 3-dimensional gameplay, where you run, jump and fly between Tokyo's skyscrapers, interspersed with areas of old, linear development featuring one- or two-story Japanese houses... It's a really fun experience! Also, the setting allows authors to twist the major laws of physics at some points, and this again adds spice to the taste.

All in all, I think Ghostwire: Tokyo is worth a 7/10 mark, especially if you are enjoying open-world games where you need to collect stuff.

Hello friends! Welcome to my review of the game GHOSTWIRE TOKOYO. This is a open world game with many quests and side quests. It features lore from japan including yokai and ghosts familiar with that region. The game also features buildings from Tokoyo such as the 409 building, the tokoyo tower, and many other real life buildings set in the city of tokoyo japan. The game is split into different chapters which most consist of a open world area where you can take your time to do quests. There are also many side quests that can be done by the player to enhance their game. There are also collectibles and hidden things to find around the world. Despite being open world, this game tends to be more horror in essence compared to other open world games. There are even jump scares on some of the quests and side quests. Anyways, here are my pro and con list:

PROS:

- Open world game with horror elements.
- Many japanese lure about yokai and ghosts.
- Collectibles.
- Controller support. I used F310 logitech.
- Beautiful music.
- Very good graphics.
- The game seems to still being developed and given additional free things and new patches.


CONS:

- Sadly, this game suffered from the ubisoft same open world format, thus degrating the game using the same formula which can make the game seem boring to some people.
- Repetition of doing some things in game can cause bordom. As with all games, if you get bored, change to another game and come back to play it later.
- Very little stuttering, but otherwise worked fine.
- The game does not take long to beat. It only took me 36 hours casually to beat the game. Hardcore games might even finish the game sooner than that.

I do recommend the game because i love exploring mythology and lure of other cultures, as in this game, it is japanese lure about fantasy creatures and different ghosts.

NOTE: If you get the game, do not play the prelude chapter until after you beat this game. The storyline in the prelude ruins many aspects of the main game and is not very good in my personal opinion.

I had this game in my radar since I heard good things about it from Mutahar, about two years ago. Since then a couple of friends recommended it to me. I finally decided to play it and I'm really glad I did.

The first thing that I noticed about this game is the presentation, it feels really premium both in terms of graphics and cinematics. Ghostwire Tokyo managed to immerse me in its world like few other games could. The story is simple, Akito has a bike accident and gets possessed by a spirit, KK, and together they fight to cleanse Shibuya from a fog which turns everyone into spirits and save Akito’s sister who has been kidnapped.
I don't want to spoil anything but the story will explore much of the traditional Japanese lore about death, demons, spirits and other such creatures. There are some awesome set pieces and in general it really got me on my toes. At the end it gets a bit emotional and I also really appreciated the ending.

The gameplay is a classic action adventure open world where we will follow a main storyline, but we'll also have tons of stuff to do, from secondary missions to collectibles of any kind. I appreciated a lot of the secondary missions, some of them are really interesting. There's one in particular which takes place in a school and it was really scary, it actually gave me goosebumps. It also reminded me of Silent Hill.

The map is pretty big and we'll be able to unlock chunks of it by cleansing the gates which generate the fog.
The world is filled with details, and it’s very explorable, both horizontally and vertically. We can indeed climb all buildings, and glide from roof to roof in order to further explore and collect all the items. 

KK will give us powers, so we pretty much have gun fingers and shoot out energy. The animations are pretty cool, and although at first they are a bit slow, by leveling up we'll be able to upgrade our moves and make them faster and more lethal. 

This game is also VERY Japanese, almost as Japanese as the Yakuza series. For someone like me who is really fascinated by that culture I find it fantastic, since it's filled to the brim with typical Japanese stuff, from the foods and drinks, to a lot of traditional objects, cats, buildings, music, and the list goes on.

Speaking about music, the soundtrack is great, with pumping music when the action kicks in and very epic pieces overall. I'm not an expert and it's always hard for me to talk about music, but all I can say is that it really fits and once again it has some great Japanese vibes.

In the technical compartment I had some really high highs and some really low lows. Let's start with the positives, the graphics are insanely good looking, and the world is a joy to look at. Having a pretty capable machine I tried cranking everything up, and for a while it seemed ok, but when I started unlocking big chunks of the open world the troubles began. 
Basically the game ran smoothly with everything maxed and TSR upscaling at 1440p, but I eventually started experiencing freezes as if I was running out of VRAM. Checking my VRAM utilization I noticed it was capped at 12 GB even though I have 16 available. Eventually I tried lowering some settings and ended up using the optimized settings by Digital Foundry with some tweaks. In the end, despite the vram utilization was still hard capped at 12 GB, I managed to get a freeze-free experience which arguably looked even better than before, since disabling ray traced shadows allowed me to also disable TSR and play at native 1440p with 60 fps. All in all I'm pretty happy with the results, even though in that department the game could have benefitted from some more time in the oven.

I played about 20 hours and completed the main story and roughly half of the other open world activities and side quests. I'm really happy with the experience and I could have continued a bit more, but ultimately I like to move on from games. Despite the technical issues, this is an amazing game and I recommend picking it up, especially if you like anything Japan related!

The game is set in a near-future Tokyo, where a mysterious phenomenon has caused 99% of the population to vanish. The player takes on the role of a paranormal investigator who must use their supernatural abilities to fight against the ghostly creatures that have invaded the city. The game features a first-person perspective and a combat system that allows the player to use hand gestures to cast spells and perform attacks. The game also incorporates elements of Japanese folklore and urban legends, creating a unique and immersive atmosphere. Ghostwire Tokyo is expected to be released for PlayStation 5, Steam and Game Pass.

PROS

- The side quests are decent though a bit too simple/easy

CONS

- The gameplay is repetitive, and unoriginal. The enemies are all killed in a very similar manner and after you are introduced to all of them it's just a repetition of the same characters over and over again.
- The storyline is extremely short. If you focus only on the main quest you can finish it in 10 hours. Not a great value if you ask me. Also, it's a linear story and there's no choices, therefore no replayability.
- The characters are forgettable, you never really feel any sympathy for what's happening to them. The main character is very vanilla, and zero customizing options besides some outfits.
- This game is a completionist nightmare. In order to platinum the game you have to spend endless hours doing chore-like activities which in no way make the game more interesting or challenging. Specially since there are randomly triggered situations of which you have no control.
- Is marketed as horror despite not being scary at all, eerie at best
- The money system is pointless given that there are not many things to buy (and too many useless things like emotes and music).
- You can only carry a maximum of 20 arrow, AFTER buying all of the perks

Ghostwire: Tokyo is a hauntingly beautiful, unique experience. Given that this was developed by Tango Gameworks—the same team behind The Evil Within—you can easily see their fingerprints all over this game. However, this version of Shibuya is so distinct that it completely sets itself apart from its spiritual ancestors. Even with its flaws, I walked away seeing immense potential for any future Ghostwire games.

As a pretty big fan of atmosphere, the game does an excellent job of maintaining a tense, eerie vibe. The emphasis leans far more toward action than pure horror—I’d pin it at roughly 65% action and 35% horror—but the rare jump scares it does throw at you feel completely fair and earned. The Shinto folklore and modernized urban legends are easily among the best aspects of the experience. My one major complaint, though, is the lack of enemy variety. Because you spend so much time in this universe, fighting the same handful of redundant supernatural designs starts to wear thin over a full playthrough.

To be clear, the core combat definitely leans into style over substance, but the visual execution of the hand-gesture magic is fun enough that I wasn't too mad about it. I actually think the community's general boredom with the combat loop stems from the camera choice. In my experience, players tend to lodge these specific repetition complaints much more often when a game locks them into a rigid first-person perspective rather than letting them view the flashy action from a third-person angle.

What often gets overlooked in the broader discussion is that the story has significantly more teeth than the marketing material led on. At its core, this is a narrative about deep grief and acceptance, launching our protagonist into an unintentional journey of self-healing. His evolving relationship and banter with KK became a surprisingly comforting anchor throughout my time exploring the empty streets. And by the end, I was in tears. 

Overall, Ghostwire: Tokyo isn't a perfect game, and it does fall into some repetitive open-world habits. I picked it up on sale for $40 and felt that price was pretty fair for what it offers. If you can look past the mechanical redundancy, the incredible setting, emotional narrative weight, and sheer artistic style make it well worth experiencing.

The game had so much potential, but it failed to live up to it. The story was fine, but the powers felt limiting. The talismans were a nice touch, but the lack of variety in abilities left me feeling unfulfilled. 

And for a game about ghost and yokais, the only truly scary location was the newly added school mission, with the rest of the game falling flat in terms of fear factor.

The side missions got repetitive quickly, and the lack of unique enemies in the open world led to a feeling of monotony. Overall, the game feels mediocre and fails to engage me for long. The game's aesthetic is a bright spot, but its reliance on the Ubisoft open world formula make for a lackluster experience that's hard to recommend to some impatient gamer.

it's a beautiful but "boring-ish" game

Ghostwire: Tokyo is a game that I've finished multiple times on different devices, and that being the case it's time to write a review for it. In order to keep this review short, I'll just mention a quick list of the goods and the bads according to my experience.

[h3]The Pros:[/h3]
[b]1. Setting[/b]
- I have to mention this at #1 because it was the main thing which made me interested in Ghostwire: Tokyo.
- Just love the use of Japanese Urban Legends and the overall theme of the game.
[b]2. Collectibles[/b]
- I know it's weird to praise collectibles, but the way it has been implemented here is really good.
- Being able to directly or indirectly track all collectibles in the game is a completionist's dream come true.
[b]3. Combat[/b]
- Ghostwire: Tokyo's take on combat is pretty interesting, and I loved the flexibility offered through it.
- During mid-to-late game, I actually had to use all elemental weaving skills to effectively tackle fights.
- This means that devs actually gave thought to the system, and there's no "one size fits all" scenario.
[b]4. Visuals[/b]
- While Ghostwire: Tokyo doesn't boast hyper-realistic UE5 graphics some new games boast today, the overall art style and graphics worked highly in favor of its immersive experience

[h3]The Cons:[/h3]
[b]1. Enemy Diversity[/b]
- While the new DLC has added a handful of extra mobs to the base game, overall there's not much variety
- Fighting the same few enemies became a bit boring, and I ended up skipping most fights if I didn't need XP
[b]2. Voice Acting[/b]
- While the story overall was pretty neat, I can't say the same for voice acting, especially the MC Akito's
- Instead of giving a natural vibe to the narratives, they felt either bland or had exaggerated emotions

[h3]Summary:[/h3]
Overall I loved both the story and the gameplay of Ghostwire: Tokyo, and would highly recommend it to other users. The main selling point of the game for me would be the setting, just loved that and the overall theme.
